transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I guess... I mean, what made me come in is just this feeling that I can't shake. It's like I'm constantly carrying around this weight, you know? I just keep feeling like I ruined things for everybody. And it's not just one thing, it's everything. Especially at work. I'm a pipefitter apprentice, and lately, I just feel like a total fake. Like I don't belong there and I'm just fooling everyone. I'll make a mistake—something small, something I know the other guys would just fix, laugh off, and move on from—but for me, it's like the end of the world. I dwell on it. I feel like I'm letting the journeymen down, letting the younger apprentices down because I'm supposed to be setting a good example, and I'm just... not. And then I take that feeling home, and I feel like I'm letting my family down, too. It's just this constant, heavy guilt over things that probably aren't even that big of a deal to anyone else, but in my head, it's like I've completely messed everything up for everyone around me. I just can't stop thinking about how I'm a burden and how I'm failing everyone.
How long have you been feeling this way?

Well, let me think... it's been a while, honestly. I'd say this whole depressed stretch, this heavy feeling, has been with me for about nine months now. It started back in the spring, I think. At first, I tried to just push through it, you know? Like, I'd wake up feeling like I was walking through molasses, but I'd force myself to get dressed, get my boots on, and get to the job site. I thought maybe I was just tired, or maybe the apprenticeship was just getting to me because it's a lot of physical work and a lot to learn all at once. I tried to hide it, put on a brave face for the crew. But then, as the months went on, it just got heavier. It became a lot harder to hide once my classes for my associate's degree started slipping, and then my work on the site started getting sloppy because I just couldn't focus. I'd be staring at a blueprint and it was like my brain was just full of static. And that's when the guilt really started piling on, making everything worse. So yeah, about nine months of just... dragging this around with me every single day.
Have you ever felt this way before, like you're carrying a heavy weight and feeling guilty about everything, in the past before these nine months started?

No, I don't think so. I mean, I've had bad days, sure. Everyone has bad days, right? Especially when you're starting out in a trade, you mess up a cut or you misread a schematic and you feel dumb for a day or two. But this... this is different. I've never had it just hang around like this, like a dark cloud that follows me everywhere. Before this spring, I was actually doing really well. I was keeping up with my classes, I was learning a lot on the site, I felt like I was really getting the hang of things and finding my place with the crew. I used to actually look forward to going to work and learning something new. I never used to feel this... this crushing sense that I'm just fundamentally wrong, you know? Like, before, if I made a mistake, I'd just think, "Okay, that was stupid, I'll do better next time." But now, a mistake means I'm a failure and I'm dragging everyone down. So, no, this whole nine-month stretch is completely new for me. It's like I woke up one day and my whole brain just switched tracks and I can't find my way back to how I used to be. It's really scary, honestly, because I don't know why it started or how to make it stop, and I just keep thinking about how I used to be able to handle things and now I just... can't.
Do you still enjoy activities or hobbies that you used to find pleasurable before these nine months started?

I used to, yeah. I really used to. But lately... no. It's actually one of the things that bothers me the most, if I'm being honest. Like, before all this started, I was always doing something. I used to love drawing, for instance. I had this sketchbook I'd carry around, mostly just doing pencil sketches, sometimes charcoal if I was feeling ambitious. I'd sketch tools, or the way the pipes looked before we covered them up, or just random things I saw on my commute. It was how I relaxed. And I played volleyball, too. Just a rec league, nothing crazy, but we played every Tuesday night and it was so much fun. I loved the team, I loved the energy, just running around and sweating out the stress of the day. And on top of that, I used to volunteer a couple of weekends a month with this local group that helps fix up houses for elderly folks in the neighborhood. I felt really good about that, using my trade skills to actually help people who needed it. 

But now... it's like a switch flipped. I'll walk right past my sketchbook sitting on the kitchen counter, and I don't even have the slightest urge to pick it up. It just looks like a chore. And volleyball? I haven't been in months. I just stopped showing up. The girls text me, asking where I am, if I'm okay, and I just... I can't even bring myself to reply sometimes. I just ignore the group chat. Same with the volunteer group. They'll send out the schedule for the month, and I just delete the email. And the weirdest part is, I don't even feel bad about missing it in the moment. I just feel... nothing. It's like those things used to be the core of who I was outside of work, the things that actually made me feel like myself, and now I just couldn't care less about them. It's so exhausting just getting through the workday that by the time I have free time, the thought of doing anything that requires effort, even things I used to love, just feels impossible. I just sit there and think about how I should want to do those things, but the want is just completely gone.
Do you still find any pleasure in the things you do on a daily basis?

Honestly, like I was kind of just saying a second ago, not really. It's all tied together, honestly. Because my daily routine is just so empty now. Like, lately I can walk right past my sketchbook sitting there on the counter, skip volleyball entirely, and just ignore the volunteer group texts lighting up my phone without feeling much of anything at all. And it blows my mind sometimes when I stop to think about it, because those used to be the things that made me feel like myself, you know? They gave my week a rhythm and a purpose. 

But now, because that's gone, even the little everyday things don't give me any sort of boost either. I used to really enjoy just getting my coffee at the drive-thru before hitting the job site, or sitting on a bucket eating my lunch and joking around with the other apprentices about whatever messy pipe layout we were dealing with that day. I used to get a kick out of that stuff, just the daily banter. Now? I just sit there chewing my sandwich, staring at the concrete, just waiting for the break to be over so I can go back to working and not talking. I don't laugh at their jokes, I don't care about the coffee... it's just all gray. It's like the color has been washed out of my whole day, from the minute my alarm goes off to the minute I go back to sleep. I just go through the motions of getting dressed, driving to the site, doing the work, coming home... and there's just zero spark in any of it. So yeah, no pleasure at all, really. Just... existing, I guess.
Have you ever thought about harming yourself or wished you were dead during these nine months?

Well... I mean, it's not like I'm sitting around making a plan or anything. I don't have some specific idea of how I would hurt myself, or like, a date picked out or anything like that. I want to be really clear about that, because I know people get worried when you start talking about this stuff, and I don't want anyone thinking I'm about to do something drastic. But... yeah, the thoughts are there. It's more of this creeping, heavy feeling that just kind of settles in when I'm alone. 

Like, especially when I'm driving home after my evening classes. The roads are usually pretty quiet, and it's dark, and I'm just so unbelievably drained from trying to keep it together all day on the site and then sitting through a lecture. I'll just be gripping the steering wheel, staring at the headlights coming the other way, and this thought will just slide into my head, like, "What if I just... didn't have to do this tomorrow?" It's not that I want to drive off the road, but just this intense wish that everything would just stop. 

And it happens at night, too, when I'm lying awake. I'll just be staring at the ceiling, listening to the hum of the refrigerator or whatever, and my brain just starts spinning. I'll think about how exhausting the next day is going to be, how I have to get up and pretend to care about the pipe layouts and make small talk with the crew, and I just get this overwhelming feeling that it would be so much easier if I just didn't wake up tomorrow. Just... if I went to sleep and that was it. No more dragging myself out of bed, no more feeling like a failure, no more of this gray, empty feeling. It's like my brain is just looking for an exit door because the room is too heavy to stand in anymore. It scares me a little, honestly, because I never used to think like that. I used to be excited for the next day. But now, it's just this constant, quiet wish for it all to just be over, even though I don't actually want to, you know, take action to make it happen. It's just a wish for relief.
Are these feelings of guilt and being a burden to others something you experience for most of the day, or are they more sporadic?

It's... well, it's pretty much most of the day. It really doesn't go away. In fact, that's really what made me come in here to see you in the first place, if I'm being completely honest. I just couldn't handle the weight of it anymore. I keep having this overwhelming feeling that I've just ruined things for everybody. It's like this constant loop in my head. 

Especially at work... I just feel like a total fake in the apprenticeship. Like I don't actually belong there and everyone is finally going to realize it. I'll make a mistake—like, maybe I cut a piece of PVC too short or I don't get a joint sealed perfectly on the first try—and I know, logically, that other people would probably just fix it, toss the bad piece in the scrap pile, and move on from it without a second thought. It's a job site, mistakes happen all the time. But for me, it just spirals. I can't let it go. 

And then I start feeling like I'm letting my family down, because they were so incredibly proud of me for getting into this trade and going after my associate's, and here I am, just feeling like a complete fraud who's wasting everyone's time. And it's not just them, it's the younger apprentices too. There are a couple of first-years who sometimes ask me for advice or watch how I do things, and I just look at them and think about how much I'm letting them down by being such a mess. I'm supposed to be someone they can learn from, and instead, I'm just agonizing over these tiny screw-ups that shouldn't even matter. So yeah, to answer your question, it's not sporadic at all. It's just this heavy, guilty feeling that I drag around with me for the entire day, telling me I'm a burden to my crew, my family, just... everyone.
Are there any activities that you still find pleasure in?

I know we touched on this a little bit a few minutes ago, but honestly... no. Not really. I think I'm still just stuck on what I was saying before, because it really is just a total blank for me right now. 

Like I mentioned with my sketchbook—I used to carry that thing literally everywhere with me. I'd draw out complicated pipe layouts just to practice for my classes, or I'd sketch random stuff if I was sitting at a coffee shop. I had all my specific shading pencils laid out, the whole nine yards. But lately, I can just walk right past it sitting there on the kitchen counter. It’s been sitting in the exact same spot for weeks, right next to the mail, and I don't even have the slightest urge to pick up a pen. I just look at it and feel... nothing. 

And it's the exact same story with volleyball. I used to play in this rec league on Thursday nights, and it was my absolute favorite part of the week. I loved the energy of it, you know? The physical exertion, diving on the floor, high-fiving everyone, just sweating it out after a long day on the job site. Now, I just skip it entirely. I don't even bother making up excuses anymore, I just don't go. I don't miss the court, I don't miss the game. 

Same with my volunteer group. My phone will be sitting there on the passenger seat of my truck, just lighting up over and over and over with group texts about organizing the weekend drive or whatever, and I just completely ignore them. I used to be the first one to reply to those! I used to be the one organizing the spreadsheets and getting everyone hyped up. Now I just watch the screen light up and I don't feel much of anything at all. No desire to join in, no excitement... just this flat, empty feeling. 

It’s just so incredibly bizarre and frustrating to me, because those used to be the things that made me feel like myself. They were my entire identity outside of just being an apprentice and going to my associate's classes. They were *me*. And without them, I just don't know what I'm supposed to enjoy anymore, or who I even am when I'm not working. So, yeah, even trying to think hard about it right now... there really isn't anything I'm finding pleasure in. It's all just kind of faded away on me.
Have you ever experienced a period of significant depression like this before in your life?

No, honestly, I haven't. And I think that's why this is all so... terrifying? Or just really confusing, honestly. Because normally, I'm the person who just bounces back from everything. 

Like, back in high school, or even when I first started my associate's program and the apprenticeship at the same time—which was a massive adjustment, by the way. I mean, waking up at 4:30 in the morning to get to the job site, hauling tools around, getting covered in PVC primer and pipe dope all day, and then rushing to sit in night classes... it was exhausting, sure. I'd have days where I was stressed out of my mind. I remember this one time I was just sobbing in my truck because I bombed a math quiz and then my journeyman had yelled at me earlier that day for threading a pipe wrong. But that was just normal stress, you know? It was situational. I'd get upset, maybe vent to my mom or text my friends about it, sleep it off, and the very next morning I was totally fine and ready to go again. 

I always had this drive. I was always the one pushing forward, always the upbeat one on the crew. So to feel like *this*... this constant, heavy, gray fog that just won't lift... it's completely new to me. I've never had a time where I couldn't just shake it off or push through it with enough caffeine and willpower. I've never had months go by where I just felt this completely empty and useless. It's like I don't even recognize the person I am right now, because the old me, the me from literally just a year ago, would never be sitting around ignoring her volleyball group or wishing she wouldn't wake up. So, no, I've never been through anything remotely close to this before in my entire life. It's my first time feeling like my brain is just... broken, I guess. Which is why I finally made the appointment, because I just don't know how to fix it myself.
Have you had more than one period where you felt significantly depressed like this in your life, even if they were separated by periods of feeling okay?

No, no, like I was just trying to say, this is literally the very first time anything like this has ever happened to me. There haven't been any other periods at all. 

I mean, I've had weeks in the past where I was just totally drained, you know? Like last winter, we were working on this massive commercial install, and the heating wasn't even hooked up in the building yet. I was freezing my hands off every single day, coming home with my knuckles completely raw and cracked from wrenching steel pipe in the cold. And yeah, I'd get home, take a boiling hot shower, and just crash. I'd be grumpy, maybe snap at my mom because I was just so physically exhausted and I still had to write a paper for my intro to business class. But that wasn't... it wasn't *this*. 

I never had a whole stretch of time where I felt like this heavy, guilty, empty shell. Once that rough job was done, or even just once Friday afternoon hit and we packed up the gang boxes, I was right back to going to the rec center for volleyball or grabbing food with the other apprentices. There was never a time in my past where I felt okay, and then plunged into this dark hole for weeks, and then felt okay again. It's always just been a steady baseline for me, just the normal, everyday ups and downs of being a twenty-year-old trying to balance a heavy-duty trade and a college degree. 

So, no, definitely not more than one period. I haven't had anything like that happen before. It's just this one single stretch, right now, that just seems like it's never going to end.
Are there any small things that still bring you joy?

I mean, I know I kind of just went on a whole rant about this a few minutes ago, but... no. Not even the small things. 

Like, if you think about what I was saying before with my sketchbook? That was just a tiny, everyday thing for me. It wasn't some huge production, it was just me sitting there with a pencil, shading in a PVC fitting or doodling while I waited for my truck to warm up in the morning. And lately, like I said, I can just walk right past it. It's just sitting there on the counter, right where I left it, and I don't feel a single spark of wanting to touch it. 

And the volunteer group texts... I mean, that's a small thing, right? Just reading a message on a screen or sending a quick thumbs-up emoji. But I just completely ignore them without feeling much of anything at all. Same with skipping volleyball—even the small parts of that, like joking around in the parking lot while putting our gear in the trunk... I just don't care about it anymore. 

It really messes with my head, honestly, because even though they might seem like small things to someone else, or just silly little hobbies, those were the things that made me feel like myself. They were what made me a person outside of just being an exhausted apprentice covered in pipe dope all day. So if you're asking if maybe I still get a little bit of joy out of, I don't know, a really good cup of coffee or listening to a favorite song on the radio on the way to the site... no. Not really. It's all just completely blank, big things and small things alike.
Do you still enjoy spending time with friends or family?

Honestly, it kind of ties right back into what I was just saying about the group texts and volleyball. Because those *are* my friends, you know? The girls on the team, the people I volunteer with... we used to be so tight. But lately, like I mentioned, I can just completely ignore those volunteer group texts. My phone will light up, I'll see their names, and I just... I don't feel anything. I don't even have the urge to type out a quick 'haha' or make up an excuse for why I can't hang out. I just leave them on read. 

And with my family... well, I live with my mom, and usually, we're super close. Normally I'd come home from the job site, completely exhausted, smelling like sweat and PVC glue, and I'd sit right down at the kitchen island and just talk her ear off about my day. I'd tell her about whatever my journeyman yelled about, or the crazy thing that happened in my intro to business class. But now? I just walk right past her. I go straight to my room and shut the door. 

It's exactly like how I can just walk past my sketchbook now, or skip volleyball without a second thought. I can just ignore all these people and these activities without feeling much of anything at all. And that's the part that really bothers me, because being around my friends, joking around with my mom, doing my volunteer stuff... those used to be the things that made me feel like myself. I was always the loud, social one! I was the glue in my friend group. Now, it just takes way too much energy to even pretend to care when my mom asks how my day was. I just give her a one-word answer. I just want to be left alone in the quiet, even though I know I'm completely shutting out everyone who actually cares about me.
Have you had any periods of depression like this before that lasted for a while and then got better on their own?

I know you kind of asked me something really similar just a few minutes ago, about having more than one period like this, and... I really meant what I said then. No. I haven't. I've never had a stretch like this before, ever. 

It's just so foreign to me. Like, I was trying to explain how I've been tired before—like that horrible winter install where I thought my fingers were going to literally snap off from the cold, and I was just so physically wiped out that I couldn't function. But even then, I never felt this... this heaviness. I never had a time where I just sank into this awful, empty place for weeks on end and then magically snapped out of it. 

I've always just been me, you know? Just going to work, going to class, hanging out with my mom, playing volleyball. My mood has always just been pretty steady. I mean, sure, I get stressed when finals are coming up and my journeyman is breathing down my neck about a tight deadline, but that's just normal stress. It passes as soon as the test is over or the job is done. I've never had a depression like this that just settled over me like a heavy blanket and stayed there. So, no, there hasn't been a time in the past where I felt like this and then it just got better on its own. This is the very first time, and honestly, that's why it's scaring me so much, because I don't know if it *is* going to get better on its own. It feels like it's just never going to end.
Have you had any other episodes of depression in your life that were similar to what you're experiencing now?

I mean... I feel like I'm repeating myself a little bit here, but honestly, no. Never. Like I was just saying about how I've never had a stretch like this that got better on its own... I've just never had a stretch like this at all. Not ever. 

I know it probably sounds weird because I'm twenty and people my age are supposed to be, I don't know, moody or whatever, but I've always been so level. Even when I was a teenager in high school, and all my friends were having these massive meltdowns over boys or grades or whatever drama was happening in the group chat... I was always the one talking them down. I was the grounded one. I was always just focused on getting through my classes and figuring out what trade I wanted to go into. I never went through a phase where I couldn't get out of bed, or where I stopped caring about things. 

Like, I can remember this one time my senior year, my dog died. Buster. He was this big, goofy golden retriever mix we'd had since I was little, and I was devastated. I cried for days, and I didn't want to go to school, and I just wanted to lay on the couch with my mom and watch sad movies. But that was grief, you know? It made sense. I was sad because I lost my dog. But even then, I still wanted to talk to my friends. I still cared about my future. I still felt like *me*, just a really sad version of me. 

But this? This is entirely different. This isn't grief, because nothing happened to trigger it. It's just this heavy, blank nothingness that completely swallowed me up out of nowhere. I've never experienced anything even remotely similar to this in my entire life. It's like I woke up one morning and someone had just unplugged me from the wall. So, yeah, no other episodes, nothing like this, not ever. This is completely, one hundred percent new territory for me, and it's awful.
Have you had more than one episode of depression in your life that lasted for at least two weeks?

I feel like I'm a broken record here, and I'm sorry, I know you have to ask these things in all these different ways to make sure you get the full picture, but... no. I really, truly haven't. Like I've been saying, this is the very first time I've ever felt anything close to this. I've never had a two-week stretch, or a one-week stretch, or a month-long stretch of feeling like this before. 

It's just so strange because I keep trying to rack my brain, trying to think if maybe I missed something in the past. Like, was there a time in high school when I was just really quiet for a few weeks and didn't notice? But no, my mom would have noticed. She's always been so tuned into me. If I had spent two whole weeks just coming home and staring at the wall like I do now, she would have marched me right to a doctor back then. But that never happened because I was always just busy. Between school, and then starting my apprenticeship, and my business classes, and volleyball... I never had the time or the inclination to just shut down for weeks at a time. 

Even when things got really stressful, like when I first started my apprenticeship and I was the youngest person on the crew and the only girl, and I had to prove myself every single day... I was exhausted, sure. I'd come home with my muscles aching so bad I could barely lift my arms to wash my hair. But I never felt this mental exhaustion. I never had a period where my brain just felt like it was full of concrete for two weeks straight. So, yeah, to answer your question, no. I've never had more than one episode of this, because this right now, what I'm going through right this second, is the first and only time it's ever happened.
Have you had any periods of feeling normal or close to your old self since this depression started about nine months ago?

No, not really. I mean, I try to act like it sometimes, you know? Like, when I'm around my mom, I try to put on a brave face because I know she worries. She's always been a worrier, especially since it's just the two of us. So I'll try to smile and ask her about her day and pretend that I'm present, but inside, I'm just... I'm not there. It's like I'm watching myself go through the motions from behind a pane of frosted glass. 

And at work, too, I try to fake it. I have to, right? You can't just be completely checked out when you're working with heavy pipes and blowtorches and stuff. You have to be focused. But it takes every ounce of energy I have just to string a sentence together and act like the old me, the girl who used to joke around with the guys on the crew and actually cared about doing a good job. 

But as far as actually *feeling* normal? Actually feeling like myself? No. Not for nine months. It's just been this constant, unending slog. There hasn't been a single day where I woke up and thought, "Oh, there I am. I'm back." It's just been this same heavy, gray feeling, day in and day out, without any break at all. Even on the days where maybe I manage to laugh at a joke or something, it doesn't reach my eyes, you know? It's just a reflex. The real me, the one who used to have energy and goals and actually enjoyed life... she hasn't made an appearance since this whole thing started. It's just been one long, continuous stretch of feeling like a ghost of myself.
Have you had any periods where your depression symptoms significantly improved for at least a few weeks before returning?

I feel like I'm just repeating the same thing over and over, and I'm really sorry if it's frustrating, but... no. No, I haven't. Like I was just saying about how I haven't felt normal at all, there hasn't been any kind of break. Not for a few weeks, not for a few days, not even for a few hours, honestly. 

It's not like the volume gets turned down for a while and I can breathe, and then it gets cranked back up. It's just been blasting at the exact same level since it started. I keep thinking about how people talk about depression coming in waves, you know? Like, you have a bad patch, and then you come up for air, and then maybe you go under again. But for me, it's just been like... I don't know, being at the bottom of the ocean. The pressure is just constant. 

I actually remember reading an article online a few months ago—well, "reading" is a strong word, I was mostly just staring at my phone screen while lying in bed—but it was about how some people have these seasonal things, or they have triggers that make them feel worse, and then they bounce back for a bit. And I remember thinking, "Wow, what must that be like?" Because I haven't bounced back at all. There hasn't been a single window of time where I thought, "Okay, the fog is lifting, I can finally focus on work again, I can finally go to the gym without feeling like my limbs are made of lead." 

My mom keeps hoping for it, too. Every time I manage to, I don't know, eat a full meal or actually put on real clothes instead of sweatpants, I can see this look in her eye, like she's thinking, "Is this it? Is she getting better?" And it breaks my heart, because I know she wants me to have those periods of improvement, and I want them too, so badly, but they just haven't happened. It's just been one long, uninterrupted slog since the very beginning. So, yeah, no breaks, no improvements for a few weeks, nothing like that at all. Just the same heavy feeling, day after day after day.
Have you ever had an episode of depression that lasted for at least two weeks, and then completely went away, before this current episode started?

I know I must sound like a broken record, and I really, truly apologize if I'm making your job harder by just saying the same thing over and over again, but... no. I haven't. Like I was trying to explain before, this current episode—this awful, heavy, nine-month-long nightmare—is the very first time I've ever experienced anything like this in my entire life. So there couldn't have been an episode that went away before this, because there was no "before this" when it comes to feeling this way.

I've been trying to think back, you know? Replaying my whole life in my head, from middle school all the way through getting my associate's degree and starting my apprenticeship. And sure, I had bad days. Everyone has bad days. I remember when I failed my first practical exam in my pipefitting class—I was devastated. I went home and cried, and I was in a terrible mood for a couple of days. I didn't want to talk to anyone, not even my mom. But that was just a reaction to something that happened, and it only lasted a few days before I picked myself up, studied harder, and passed the retake. It wasn't this... this sickness. It wasn't a two-week stretch of feeling completely hollowed out and hopeless. 

And then there was the time my dog died when I was sixteen. That was heartbreaking. I was sad for a long time, but it was a normal kind of sad, you know? I still went to school, I still went to volleyball practice, I still hung out with my friends, even if I wasn't as bubbly as usual. It never turned into an episode where I couldn't function or where I felt like my brain was moving through molasses for weeks on end. 

So, yeah, I've never had a depression that lasted two weeks and then went away, because I've never had depression before this at all. This is the first time the switch flipped, and unfortunately, it hasn't flipped back since. It's just been this one, massive, continuous thing. I really wish I could say yes, that I had it before and it went away, because then at least I'd have some proof that it *can* go away, you know? That I can get back to normal. But since this is the first time, I don't even have that reassurance. It's just... no, this is the first and only time.
Have you ever had an episode of depression that completely went away before this current episode started?

Wait, I'm sorry, didn't... didn't you just ask me that? Or something really similar? I know my brain is kind of moving in slow motion these days and I'm rambling a lot, but I feel like we just talked about this. But, um, yeah, the answer is still no. I've never had an episode that went away before this one started, because I've never had an episode before this one at all. 

Like I was saying, this is the very first time my brain has ever done anything like this to me. Before nine months ago, I was always the person with almost too much energy, you know? Back when I was finishing my associate's degree, I was juggling all my classes, doing my apprenticeship hours, and helping my mom keep the apartment together, and I never crashed. I would literally wake up at 5 AM, spend eight hours hauling around heavy steel pipes and working with the guys, and still have it in me to go out or stay up late studying. 

If I had ever experienced this kind of total, paralyzing shutdown before, I would absolutely remember it. And my mom would definitely remember it, too, because I would have been completely useless to her and to my crew. But there was never a time where I couldn't get out of bed for weeks, and then suddenly I was fine again. Never. So there's no previous episode that went away. There's just... this.
